explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The Teacher says a man's wisdom brightens his face, and the sternness of his face is changed. Wisdom works like a warm oven on a cold morning, because it takes the scowl right off. Wise folks tend to look like they just remembered where they left the good cookies.

It goes the other direction, friend. The Teacher says wisdom brightens the face, and the sternness of his face is changed. So the stern look is the thing wisdom softens, not the thing it builds. Picture a scowl going soft like dough on a warm counter.

No face gets covered in this verse. The Teacher says a man's wisdom brightens his face. Wisdom turns the lights on, it doesn't pull the curtains shut. It even changes the sternness of his face, so the frown has to go.

explanations.answer: Because of your oath before God
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. The Teacher says, “Keep the king’s command, I say, because of your oath before God.” So this is about a promise made with God as the witness. A promise like that is worth keeping, friend, even when keeping it is a pain.

explanations.answer: Because the king pays your wages
explanations.explanation: Paychecks run a lot of our days, so I get the guess. But the verse gives another reason: “…because of your oath before God.” Wages never come up in it. The reason sits with a promise before God, not with the king's money box.

explanations.answer: Because the people are watching you
explanations.explanation: A crowd watching can make anybody behave, I'll give you that. But the Teacher never mentions an audience here. He says, “…because of your oath before God.” The promise is the reason, whether anybody's looking or not.

explanations.answer: He will do whatever he pleases
explanations.explanation: That's it. The Teacher says not to persist in a bad cause, “…for he will do whatever he pleases.” When one person holds the crown, pushing and pushing in front of him is a risky move. Wise folks know when to stop talking, friend, and I say that as someone with a mustache that never stops.

That would be handy for some of us, but the verse never says it. The Teacher's reason is, “…for he will do whatever he pleases.” Nothing in the text says the king's memory is the problem. The problem is that he can act however he likes.

explanations.answer: He only listens to his advisers
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say who the king listens to. The reason it gives is, “…for he will do whatever he pleases.” Advisers don't show up at all. All the Teacher points to is how much freedom the king has.

The verse says it the other way around. The Teacher says the king's word is supreme, and then asks who can say to him, what are you doing. He asks it as a question because no one is lining up to do it. So this one is false, friend, and the line behind the king isn't moving.

Yes, false. The Teacher says the king's word is supreme and asks who can say to him, what are you doing. Nobody gets to walk up and question the crown. When the king does whatever he pleases, that question is a big one to ask.
True, friend. The Teacher says, “Whoever keeps his command will come to no harm…” That's a calm promise for anyone standing before a king. Keeping the command is the safe road.

The text says the opposite of false here. The Teacher says, “Whoever keeps his command will come to no harm…” So the one who keeps the king's command is the one who stays safe. That's why the answer is true.
There it is. The Teacher says a wise heart “…knows the right time and procedure.” It's knowing when and how, not only what. A good heart reads the clock and the recipe both.

Wouldn't that be something? But the Teacher never says a wise heart knows the king's plans. He says it knows “…the right time and procedure.” Wisdom here is about timing and the right way, not spying on the palace.

That would be a heavy gift, friend, and the verse never gives it. The Teacher says a wise heart knows “…the right time and procedure.” He's talking about when and how to act. Reading minds isn't on the list.

Not quite, friend. The Teacher says, “Since no one knows what will happen, who can tell him what is to come?” So no one has the power to tell what's coming, even a wise man. Plenty of people try, but my crystal ball is just a cookie tin.

Yes, false. The Teacher says no one knows what will happen, and asks who can tell him what is to come. Even after talking about right timing, he reminds us that the future is out of our sight. A wise heart knows the time to act, but it can't see around the corner.

That's it. The Teacher says, “…so no one has authority over his day of death.” A man can't hold back the wind, and he can't hold back that day either. It's a serious thing, so I'll just say it plainly and let it sit.

The sun does come up on schedule, but the verse doesn't name it. The Teacher says no one has authority over his day of death. That's the second thing in the list, right beside the wind. It's a heavy one, so he says it straight.
Plenty of us wish we could steer a neighbor's thoughts, friend, but the Teacher never goes there. His list is the wind and the day of death. No one has authority over either one.

The verse says the reverse. The Teacher says no one can be discharged in wartime, and so wickedness will not release those who practice it. Wickedness doesn't open the door and let them walk off. Once somebody is in it, it holds on.

Right, false. The Teacher says that as no one can be discharged in wartime, “…so wickedness will not release those who practice it.” There's no walking away whenever you feel like it. It's a hard line, so I won't joke on it.

That's the one, friend. The Teacher says the wicked who used to go in and out of the holy place “…were praised in the city where they had done so.” Then he says, “This too is futile.” It's a puzzling scene, and he doesn't hide that it puzzles him.

You'd expect that, and so would I. But the Teacher says they were praised in the city where they had done so. That's the very thing that makes him call it futile. A curse would have made more sense to him.
A banishment would at least feel fair. But the Teacher says they were praised in the city where they had done so. Nobody sent them away in this scene. That's why he writes, “This too is futile.”

explanations.answer: They become fully set on doing evil
explanations.explanation: That's right. The Teacher says, “When the sentence for a crime is not speedily executed, the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil.” A slow answer to a wrong turn sends hearts further down it. It's a sobering thing to say, so I'll leave it plain.

explanations.answer: They grow more afraid of the judge
explanations.explanation: You'd think slow justice would keep folks nervous, but the verse says the opposite. The Teacher says hearts “…become fully set on doing evil.” Fear doesn't grow, the hearts do something worse. That's a hard thing to read.

explanations.answer: They learn to forgive one another
explanations.explanation: That's a kind thought, friend, but the verse doesn't go there. The Teacher says that when the sentence isn't speedily executed, “…the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil.” Forgiveness isn't mentioned at all. It's a heavy line, so I won't dress it up.

There you go. The Teacher says, “…it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence.” He says it right after noticing a sinner can do evil a hundred times and still live long. Still, he says he knows it. That's a steady word in a confusing stretch.

Honest questions about God are all through the Bible, but this verse doesn't use that word. The Teacher says it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence. The blank wants fear. That's the group he's pointing to.

Avoiding God isn't what the verse describes. The Teacher says it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence. Reverent in His presence is the opposite of staying away. The word that fits the blank is fear.

The text goes the other way, friend. The Teacher says, “…it will not go well with them, and their days will not lengthen like a shadow.” That's about the wicked because they do not fear God. So their days don't stretch out like a shadow. The answer is false.

Yes, false. The Teacher says that because the wicked do not fear God, “…it will not go well with them, and their days will not lengthen like a shadow.” Their days don't stretch out the way an evening shadow does. It's a firm word after a very confusing stretch.

explanations.answer: They get what the wicked deserve
explanations.explanation: That's what he sees. The Teacher says, “There are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve…” Then he says, “I say that this too is futile.” That one sends the eyebrows up, and I think it sent his up too.

explanations.answer: They get double the reward they earned
explanations.explanation: Wouldn't that be nice? But the Teacher sees something harder. He says there are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve. That's why he calls it futile. A double reward wouldn't have bothered him.

explanations.answer: They get honored by the king
explanations.explanation: The king isn't in this verse at all. The Teacher says there are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve. He calls that futile. An honor from the king would have been a different story.
True, friend. The Teacher says, “…and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve.” It runs both ways in that verse. That's why he says plainly that this too is futile.

The verse says it plainly, so this one is true. The Teacher says there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve. It's the other half of the same futility. Both halves are why he calls it futile.

That's what he commends. The Teacher says, “So I commended the enjoyment of life…” Then he adds that nothing is better under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry. After all that puzzling, he lands on gladness, and I like his landing.

Riches don't come up in this verse, friend. The Teacher says he commended the enjoyment of life. He says nothing is better under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry. That's a simpler joy than a bigger pile of coins.
Study is good, but the verse doesn't name it. The Teacher says he commended the enjoyment of life. Eating and drinking and being merry are what he lists. Joy is the thing he's pointing at here.

You've got it. The Teacher says this joy will go with a man “…during the days of his life that God gives him under the sun.” So the days are a gift from God, and the joy comes along on them. It's a kind thought.

Plenty of folks say chance runs the days, but that's not what the verse says. The Teacher says the days of his life are the days that God gives him under the sun. So the blank is God. Chance never gets a seat at this table.

Fortune sounds nice, friend, but the verse doesn't use it. The Teacher says the days of a man's life are days that God gives him under the sun. The blank holds God. It's a gift, not a roll of the dice.

explanations.answer: He is unable to comprehend it
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. The Teacher says he saw every work of God, and that a man is unable to comprehend the work that is done under the sun. He goes on, “Despite his efforts to search it out, he cannot find its meaning…” A man can work and work, and the whole picture stays out of reach. Honest and humble, and I like it.

explanations.answer: He can master it with effort
explanations.explanation: Effort is good, but the verse says it won't get there. The Teacher says, “Despite his efforts to search it out, he cannot find its meaning…” So a man tries and still can't comprehend it. That's the opposite of mastering it.

explanations.answer: He can explain it to others
explanations.explanation: Teaching it would be great, but the Teacher says a man is unable to comprehend the work that is done under the sun. You can't explain what you can't comprehend. Even the wise man who claims to know is unable to comprehend, he says.

The verse says the reverse, friend. The Teacher says, “…even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend.” So the claim doesn't make it so. The answer is false, and it's a humbling one.
Yes, false. The Teacher says, “…even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend.” A claim isn't the same as comprehending. Even the wise man falls short of it.
